about:
As a Chicagoland native, I’ve always been drawn to solving complex problems and helping others grow. 

Whether it’s guiding a business through a challenging problem or mentoring other students navigating their careers, I find energy in breaking down problems, uncovering opportunities, and driving meaningful impact.

With experience in consulting, technical accounting, and business strategy, I’ve worked across various industries to help organizations streamline financial operations, drive strategic initiatives, and optimize decision-making. I’ve led projects focused on financial reporting, financial modeling, and process improvements, helping businesses enhance efficiency and navigate complex transitions. I’ve also spearheaded strategic initiatives aimed at boosting customer engagement, revenue generation, and cross-functional collaboration.

Beyond my work, I’m deeply committed to mentorship and leadership coaching students on career paths, fostering inclusive communities, and leading professional development initiatives. I love collaborating with others and tackling challenges that create opportunities for growth.

At my core, I believe the best solutions come from curiosity, collaboration, and a willingness to challenge the status quo. I’m always excited to connect with others whether that's to exchange ideas, problem-solve, or simply learn from each other!

Operations & Strategy Executive with 25+ years of experience guiding Automotive and Industrial Manufacturing organizations through transformation and growth. I partner with C-suite leaders to drive strategic clarity, operational excellence, and measurable financial impact. From early Industry 4.0 modernization to today’s AI-enabled performance improvement, I’ve led initiatives delivering multi-million-dollar cost savings, accelerated product launches, and strengthened global competitiveness.

My experience spans Engineering, Product Development, Operations Strategy, and M&A, enabling a holistic approach to transformation. I’ve delivered multi-million-dollar cost savings through SG&A optimization, supply chain efficiency, and plant modernization, while helping clients launch new products in North America, pursue global market expansion, and execute strategic acquisitions.

With experience leading modernization efforts from Industry 4.0 adoption to AI-enabled operations, I now focus on helping organizations identify the right use cases and AI investments to enhance operations productivity, decision-making, and enterprise agility.

I’m passionate about helping leaders transform manufacturing and operations into digital, data-driven growth engines that define the future of industrial performance.

Focus Areas: Automotive | Commercial Vehicles | Electrification | Enterprise Cost

When clients partner with us, they don’t just stay ahead of disruption—they lead it.

publications.title: Analyzing Aqueous Solution Imbibition into Shale and the Effects of Optimizing Critical Fracturing Fluid Additives
publications.description: Two methods of hydraulic fracturing most widely utilized on unconventional shale gas and oil reservoirs are “gelled fracturing” and “slick-water fracturing”. Both methods utilize up to several million gallons of water-based fluid per well in a series of stages pumped into direct contact with subsurface rock. Shale can absorb water through a process called capillary imbibition when the two come in contact. Additionally, since a common component of shale rock is clay, water may intercalate into clay structures in the shale causing them to swell and/or break off from a fracture face, potentially plugging the desired fluid conductivity of the created fractures. Currently the extent of water-based fluid imbibition and intercalation in major shale plays is not known; however it is not uncommon for only 15 – 30% of pumped fracture fluid to return to the surface during production from a well. How these issues affect fracture conductivity and thus production from unconventional oil and natural gas wells is poorly understood. Additionally, it is not known how various fracturing fluid additives affect the magnitude of water-based fluid imbibition and/or intercalation into shale. The work our group is conducting seeks to quantify the effects of pertinent chemical additives on fluid imbibition and intercalation into shale samples. We do this with the hope that we will eventually be able to determine how natural phenomena and additives affect long term resource production from unconventional oil and natural gas wells.

Driving strategic change is hard.

More than ever before, business leaders need to be decisive in uncertain times, clear for multigenerational and diverse audiences, and dynamic when leaning into big, tough changes in how to compete and how to operate.

But potential is exciting.

As a Partner in KPMG’s Strategy Group, I advise leaders on how to drive their organisations to adapt and grow to meet their potential. I work with multinationals, Private Equity investors and starts ups who strive to give customers great products, brands or experiences.  

I’m passionate about helping make it happen.  My recipe is simple. I bring:

1. Hands-on, practical experience…
- fifteen years of working with leaders globally to navigate complexity and grow, including co-founding a fabulous business in the Middle East

2. …backed by academic rigour and insight…
- a love of understanding things at a principle and theory level, through studies at Oxford, Chicago, Beijing and Warwick

3. …to tell clear, compelling stories…
- from years of graphic design, communications and teaching students from 13-63 years old to help make big ideas stick

4. ...with a relentless focus on delivering sustainable value:

I’m always keen to exchange ideas on the consumer of the future, winning business models, and delivering complex transformations so please do get in touch.

publications.title: Remaining Competitive in the Technology Industry
publications.description:
The technology sector is experiencing tremendous, fast-paced growth. Industry players large and small are spending unprecedented amounts on R&D. Competition is fierce, causing innovation cycles to occur at an increasingly rapid pace.

The convergence of these disruptive market forces are prompting technology executives to seek new ways to compete.

It’s becoming increasingly clear that for technology companies to realize their growth aspirations, they need to accelerate the deployment of their growth strategies. about:
Arturo brings a diverse knowledge base with 13+ years of experience in audit and accounting advisory from two of the Big4 and in house accounting experience with public and private companies (including from Fortune 500). As a trusted advisor, he has assisted companies in the deal space to solve complex accounting issues under US GAAP and IFRS and integration of financial processes such as ERPs, Lease Accounting Systems, and more. Arturo is a subject matter expert on the new lease accounting standards ASC 842 and IFRS 16 and has also worked on various other accounting pronouncements such as ASC 606 Revenue Recognition, ASC 810 Consolidations, among others, for companies amongst various industries.

As a bilingual CPA, he supports companies both in the US and Latin America and effectively builds strong, trusted relationships with cross-border and cross-functional teams to communicate key financial information to decision makers, including c-level executives. My core competencies include holistic tax and trade strategic planning, transforming tax and trade operations through the use of leading technologies and processes, and evaluating and implementing Global Trade Management Technologies, such as SAP GTS and Oracle GTM. publications.title: A Woman’s Place is in the Resistance: Understanding the Legacy of Female Combatants on Post-Conflict Gender Equity
publications.description: This thesis represents the first effort to leverage quantitative methods to comprehensively understand the long-term political dynamics of female combatants in cases of civil war and insurgency. I examine the relationship between women’s participation in rebel groups and their representation in negotiations and post-conflict politics across multiple scenarios. I contend that when women actively participate in rebellion they increase the likelihood of institutionalizing women’s presence and activity in the post-conflict political environment in diverse ways. In a series of three empirical tests, I explore the effects of female combatant presence and prevalence on women’s representation on elite negotiating teams, gender provision inclusion in peace agreements, and gender quota adoption by former rebel parties. I test how the gender composition of rebel groups explains variation in women’s post-conflict political representation using cross-national data on women’s activity in 316 insurgencies active between 1964 and 2014 from the Women in Armed Rebellion Dataset 1.3 (WARD). I also utilize data on women’s participation in negotiations from Krause et al. (2018), gender provisions in peace agreements from PA-X 5 (Bell et al. 2021), and gender quotas from the IDEA Gender Quotas Database (GQD), alongside original data on gender quota adoption. I show that peace processes involving rebel groups with female combatants are significantly more likely to include women on conflict termination teams. Additionally, political parties succeeding rebel groups with female combatants are significantly more likely to voluntarily adopt party quotas, and as the share of female combatants in a group increases, the probability of party quota adoption increases. These findings support the existence of a robust relationship between rebel group and political movement as it relates to women’s representation.

publications.title: Predicting E. coli concentrations using limited qPCR deployments at Chicago beaches
publications.description: Culture-based methods to measure Escherichia coli (E. coli) are used by beach administrators to inform whether bacteria levels represent an elevated risk to swimmers. Since results take up to 12 h, statistical models are used to forecast bacteria levels in lieu of test results; however they underestimate days with elevated fecal indicator bacteria levels. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) tests return results within 3 h but are 2–5 times more expensive than culture-based methods. This paper presents a prediction model which uses limited deployments of qPCR tested sites with inter-beach correlation to predict when bacteria will exceed acceptable thresholds. The model can be used to inform management decisions on when to warn residents or close beaches due to exposure to the bacteria. Using data from Chicago collected between 2006 and 2016, the model proposed in this paper increased sensitivity from 3.4 percent to 11.2 percent–a 230 percent increase. We find that the correlation between beaches are substantial enough to provide higher levels of precision and sensitivity to predictive models. Thus, limited deployments of qPCR testing can be used to deliver better predictions for beach administrators at lower cost and less complexity.

publications.title: Machine-learned epidemiology: real-time detection of foodborne illness at scale
publications.description: Machine learning has become an increasingly powerful tool for solving complex problems, and its application in public health has been underutilized. The objective of this study is to test the efficacy of a machine-learned model of foodborne illness detection in a real-world setting. To this end, we built FINDER, a machine-learned model for real-time detection of foodborne illness using anonymous and aggregated web search and location data. We computed the fraction of people who visited a particular restaurant and later searched for terms indicative of food poisoning to identify potentially unsafe restaurants. We used this information to focus restaurant inspections in two cities and demonstrated that FINDER improves the accuracy of health inspections; restaurants identified by FINDER are 3.1 times as likely to be deemed unsafe during the inspection as restaurants identified by existing methods. Additionally, FINDER enables us to ascertain previously intractable epidemiological information, for example, in 38% of cases the restaurant potentially causing food poisoning was not the last one visited, which may explain the lower precision of complaint-based inspections. We found that FINDER is able to reliably identify restaurants that have an active lapse in food safety, allowing for implementation of corrective actions that would prevent the potential spread of foodborne illness.

about:
As a Tax Managing Director and Business License Practice Lead at KPMG, I specialize in transforming complex State and Local Tax (SALT) challenges into streamlined, technology-driven business assets. With over 25 years of experience—including 16 years focused on specialized compliance and consulting—I am dedicated to helping Fortune 500 companies navigate the shifting regulatory landscape through innovation and process excellence.
I lead with a process excellence oriented mindset, leveraging data-driven problem-solving to reduce risk and enhance operational efficiency. My career is defined by 'Tax Reimagined' initiatives, where I’ve served as a key stakeholder in developing proprietary software tools that manage thousands of licenses and permits. I am deeply committed to professional excellence, having completed hundreds of hours of continuing education across technical tax, leadership, and ethical integrity to stay at the forefront of the industry.
Beyond compliance, I am a strategic partner helping retail, telecommunications, and service-based clients optimize their business licensing and sales tax registration processes through automation and centralized management

experience.description: As a Tax Managing Director at KPMG, I serve as the Business License Practice Lead, overseeing specialized State and Local Tax (SALT) compliance and consulting for global enterprises. I am responsible for driving strategic "Tax Reimagined" initiatives by integrating advanced technology and Lean Six Sigma methodologies to automate high-volume licensing and registration processes.

about:
Gordon is a leading tax professional skilled in assisting multinationals navigate through the complexities of domestic and international M&A transactions, particularly in light of the evolving global tax environment. 

Professional and Industry Experience
Gordon’s primary areas of concentration are U.S. federal income tax considerations relating to domestic and cross-border mergers, acquisitions, spin-offs, divestitures, joint ventures, restructurings, bankruptcy and non-bankruptcy workouts, consolidated returns, and foreign tax credit, basis, earnings and profits and other tax attribute matters. He also has significant experience in the taxation of private equity funds and other collective investment vehicles as well as the taxation of complex financial arrangements and products.
Gordon has been recognized in Chambers USA, Chambers Global, Legal 500 and other publications as a leading tax individual in the United States. 

Other Activities
Gordon is currently the Second Vice-Chair of the Executive Committee of the New York Bar Association Tax Section and is a former co-chair of the New York State Bar Association Tax Section’s Committee on Reorganizations and Committee on Cross-Border Capital Markets. He is also a former chair of the American Bar Association Tax Section’s Committee on Affiliated and Related Corporations and is on the advisory board of the University of Chicago Tax Conference.
Gordon speaks frequently at professional education programs on federal income tax topics and has written extensively on corporate reorganization and other tax subjects. Among the forums at which Gordon has been a regular speaker are the American Bar Association, the D.C. Bar Association, the Federal Bar Association, the International Bar Association, the International Tax Institute, the New York State Bar Association, the Practicing Law Institute, the Southern Federal Tax Institute, the Texas Federal Tax Institute and the University of Chicago Tax Conference.

publications.title: Business Transformation and the Corporate Agenda
publications.description: Trends affecting business transformation are unprecedented in their sheer number and intensity. For corporations, change has become the new normal, according to a KPMG study of more than 900 senior executives from U.S.-based multinationals and asset managers, as well as one-on-one interviews with top executives. Business transformation has taken hold across the broad corporate landscape due to the confluence of several important triggers, including a tipping point in globalization, a major slowdown in Western economies, significant shifts in technology and energy costs, and the challenges of regulatory compliance.

publications.title: Business Transformation and the Regulatory Environment
publications.description:
The current dynamic regulatory environment is a very important trigger of transformation. Depending on the industry sector, the regulatory environment can be a partial or dominant trigger for transformation. Regulatory compliance, though a necessity spearheaded by external factors, is an opportunity to transform and catapult a company to a new level of competitive advantage. In this paper, we outline three different approaches that companies currently employ, depending on the industry, the regulations and/or the companies’ approaches to incorporating them.

New regulations often demand complex changes, but also create a big opportunity to spearhead changes in other areas of business for those companies that are able to gain a proactive view of the current and upcoming regulatory landscape. Regulatory vigilance—including regulatory elements as part of business transformation—leads to increased acuity about transformation processes. Research shows that companies that integrate regulatory issues in the transformation framework are more likely to assess their operating models against business strategy and follow better practices regarding the processes and structuring of their transformations.

publications.title: Business Transformation: People. Process. Results
publications.description:
Business transformation has taken hold across the broad corporate landscape due to the confluence of several important triggers, including a tipping point in globalization, a major slowdown in Western economies, significant shifts in technology and energy costs, and the challenges of regulatory compliance.

The key to the success of a business transformation is often in the organizational approach. Characteristics of innovative approaches to transformation include:
• Having a formal process for prioritizing business transformation initiatives
• Using a combination of an executive committee and a working team to prioritize transformation initiatives
• Handling transformation in a centralized, top-down manner 
• Having a dedicated internal organization to handle transformation

publications.title: From Burden to Competitive Advantage: Regulatory Change and Transformation in Financial Services
publications.description:
For companies in the financial services sector, the challenges of the current global regulatory environment are twofold: Regulations are expensive to implement, and they can limit revenue growth and profitability. Thus, to gain competitive advantage through a transformation, financial services firms need to design strategy and an operating model based on a regulatory framework.

Linking how you’re addressing regulatory issues along with the business strategy is incredibly important. That is a differentiator for the financial services firms that get transformation right. In this paper, we address three important steps that need to be taken to achieve a successful regulatory transformation.

publications.title: WEBCAST: Business Transformation and the Corporate Agenda
publications.description: This January 2014 webcast explores the types of business transformations being undertaken by companies today and the confluence of factors that triggered them. It also discusses how executives and thought leaders approach the strategy and execution of a business transformation in their organizations.

publications.title: Demographics and Graffiti Occurrences in Comparison to Gang Presence Across Chicago
publications.publishedAt: Loyola University Undergraduate Research and Engagement Symposium · Apr 1, 2020
publications.description: Graffiti is a popular stamp all over the City of Chicago. While graffiti is evenly spread over the city limits, there are prospective social indicators that might signify a higher presence of the artwork. Through data modeling techniques, one can compare the social demographics of median income, highest occurring age range, and population density with the location of graffiti throughout the various zip codes. By conducting an analysis to discover the demographics that correlate the highest to occurrences of graffiti, prescriptive analytics can be used to aid the City of Chicago with identifying neighborhoods with possible gang presence. Specifically, through the methodology of cluster analysis, predictor importance can indicate social demographics of areas more likely to experience gang presence. This information may be used to aid in correlating these demographics to gang-related areas for law enforcement purposes. The findings showed the age range of those that inhabit the zip code was the strongest indicator of graffiti occurrences in the area - those in the 25-34 age range tend to be living in areas with higher graffiti count. Another close indicator showed that lower population density correlated with higher graffiti occurrences. By overlaying this information with gang territories, there was not a strong correlation between age range and graffiti occurrences with gang presence. On the other hand, the second highest important predictor, population density, was consistent with the gang territory map of Chicago.

headline: Associate Director of Internal Communications, supporting KPMG Delivery Network (KDN) and KPMG Powered Enterprise
about:
Elizabeth is an Associate Director within Advisory Services in the Chicago office of KPMG LLP, supporting global internal communications for KPMG Powered Enterprise and the KPMG Delivery Network.  

Elizabeth's previous roles at KPMG include: three years as an Associate and Senior Associate in the Audit practice in the Boston office, two years as a Campus Development Manager in the Campus Recruiting department, three years as a Senior Associate and Manager in the Forensic practice under KPMG Risk Consulting Advisory Services, and two years in the People & Change practice under KPMG Management Consulting, both in the Chicago office.

Elizabeth’s clients have included consumer and retail,  industrial manufacturing, automotive, and technology businesses. Elizabeth interned with KPMG during the summer of 2007 and joined the firm full-time in September 2008. 

In addition to her day job, Elizabeth and her husband have a daughter, a son, and a playful pug. Her favorite role is mama to her kiddos, but she also enjoys exploring new cities, eating great food, supporting the Chicago community, and cheering on the Fighting Irish!

experience.description: Within Advisory Services, Elizabeth’s clients have included automotive, consumer markets and technology organizations. She has assisted in enterprise and compliance program development and risk assessments, investigations, internal audits and preparation for an accounting system implementation. Elizabeth has also facilitated KPMG Advisory training and assisted with course content development during a KPMG Learning & Development rotation.

As the Campus Development Manager in-charge of recruiting at the University of Notre Dame, Elizabeth acted as the single point of contact for Notre Dame campus recruits and managed all Notre Dame recruiting functions including hiring, financial budgeting, relationship development, event planning, guest lectures and executive visits.

As a member of KPMG’s Audit practice, Elizabeth provided professional audit services in accordance with U.S. GAAP.  Elizabeth’s audit experience includes work as a key member of the audit engagement teams of a public software company and a semiconductor company.  Elizabeth has also worked on the reviews and financial statement audits of a public bank and a consumer goods company.

receivedRecommendations.description:
This is an unsolicited recommendation for Brian Tam.  I had the pleasure of working with Brian during our time together at ESADE Business School in Barcelona, Spain.  We were placed together in a work group and therefore spent hours upon end together, day after day, working on projects for all of our classes.  Brian immediately fell into a leadership role and became a driving force for our group’s success.  He was always full of great ideas, would always pick up the slack if needed, and I never questioned whether or not he would deliver what he promised.  Through his funny and laid back style, he definitely helped to bond our group together, both inside and outside of the classroom.

Beyond that team experience, and what I remember most fondly about Brian, was the time we spent together after class in an informal study session.  A natural whiz at finance, statistics and accounting, he selflessly offered to tutor a group of us who did not have the natural talent he did in these subjects.  He would patiently spend hours at the dry erase board, giving each of us the attention we needed, and was always eager to answer any and all questions, no matter how small or big.  And best of all, he always did this with a smile and never complained.  If it wasn’t for Brian sacrificing the little free time he had between classes, projects and meetings, I truly believe that we would not have performed as well as we did.  

I have complete confidence in Brian’s abilities to consistently deliver and know that he will be a top contributor at any company that is lucky enough to snatch him up!

projects.title: Digital Marketing Consulting Project: Marie’s Waco
projects.description:
As a requirement for Baylor University's senior-level "Digital Marketing" course (MKT 4350), my team of three undergraduate students and I were tasked with completing a semester-long project: designing an original brand identity and marketing campaign for Marie’s, a soon-to-open Wine bar in downtown Waco, Texas. Because Marie’s was a brand new business, they had not developed any digital presence, giving us complete freedom to create something from the ground up.

Our final deliverable was a 25-minute presentation given to the owner of Marie’s via Zoom. This presentation included an in-depth competitive analysis; target audiences and customer personas; visual branding guidelines; a detailed digital content strategy (including Instagram, Facebook, Pinterest, influencer collaborations, email, SEO, VSO, email, website, and digital POS integration); and a complete budget. Ultimately, our team was awarded first place by our client and was adapted for actual use by Marie’s. From our professor, we received a perfect score (300/300) for the quality of our presentation and adaptation of class concepts. 

On top of my contribution to the project's content and presentation, I was appointed to be the Account Director (AKA the team leader). Therefore, I was tasked with a number of additional duties, such as managing the team's progress and quality of work, serving as our team's representative in all communications, speaking with our professor and client on behalf of the team to seek feedback and critique, and giving the final approval for all content prior to submission.

projects.title: Human Resources Staffing Project: City of Waco
projects.description:
As a requirement for Baylor University's senior-level "Human Resource Staffing and Employee Relations" course (MGT 43337), my team of three undergraduate students and I were tasked with completing a semester-long project: Working with the City of Waco, Texas, to develop and propose best practices for increasing their workforce diversity.

Our final deliverables were a 19-page report and an accompanying 15-minute presentation given to our City of Waco contacts via Zoom. This presentation was a summary of our report and included a situation analysis, an evaluation of their current diversity efforts, revised job descriptions, recommended communication/recruitment channels, human resources webpage tips, and suggestions on bolstering their hire pipeline.

As our team’s appointed data expert, I was tasked with gathering and analyzing City of Waco and US Census data to identify weak points and opportunities for growth relating to the diversity of applicants. Furthermore, I led out on the presentation of our revised job descriptions--which placed a heavy emphasis on furthering ADA inclusivity/compliance--and recommended communication/recruitment channels.

projects.title: International Marketing Consulting Project: EMEA/Germany
projects.description:
As a requirement for Baylor University's senior-level "International Marketing" course (MKT 4325), my team of three undergraduate students and I were tasked with completing a semester-long project: assume the identity of a member of the “Global Organization” (GO) and take a US-made product or service to an international market. We ultimately settled on Palantir’s Foundry and Gotham data analysis programs and decided to take our wears to Germany and the EMEA.

Our final deliverables were a simple website representing our team and a 20-minute presentation given to our professor, who assumed the role of the GO’s CEO. This presentation included an international market analysis; a competitive analysis against our classmates' teams (Japan/APAC and Brazil/Americas); a use case for our product; a detailed partnership with a German consulting company; an assessment of our potential risks and associated logistics; a ramp strategy; and a projected three-year, pro forma income statement.

As our team’s appointed financial expert, I was tasked with developing our ramp strategy and income statements. This involved estimating revenues, costs of goods sold, and other internal costs, in spite of the fact that Palantir is highly secretive and had never released any pricing information to the public. Despite this, I was personally commended for presenting the “most realistic, detailed, and useful” financial information in our class. Our team received praise for both taking a strong partner-first approach to our entrance into the German market and our prioritization of customer privacy, which related to both Palantir and Germany’s high standards for data security.

projects.title: Lunar New Year 2019
projects.description:
Lunar New Year (also known as "LNY") is an annual, all-university cultural celebration on Baylor University's campus. The event immersed community members in the diverse cultures of Asia (including South Korea, China, and Taiwan) through its cuisine, interactive art, and live music and dance performances. LNY was organized and executed through collaboration between Baylor University's Asian Student Association (ASA) and the Baylor Activities Council (BAC), reaching more than 500 people from the Baylor community in 2020.

As the BAC Marketing Coordinator for this event, I worked with BAC and ASA Program Managers to develop a positive and distinct event identity as well as create and execute various marketing strategies (physical, digital, and guerrilla) campus-wide. These included a coordinated Instagram-based social media campaign across two distinct accounts; a Chinese lantern themed guerrilla marketing effort; the creation and development of event and t-shirt logos and designs; and handheld photography/videography during the event.

projects.title: Baylor AT&T Marketing Innovation Competition
projects.description:
As a requirement for Baylor University's "Principles of Marketing" course (MGT 3305), my team of four undergraduate students and I were tasked with completing a semester-long project: designing an original product and marketing campaign for AT&T. The project required that we developed a new product and an accompanying marketing mix, specifically targeted at AT&T's target audience.

Our final deliverable was a 15-minute presentation given to a panel of AT&T Marketing Directors. This presentation included findings from original surveys, market research, an AT&T SWOT analysis, a competition analysis, estimated production costs for our product, a commercial, a sample website, and an argument as to how our product aligned with AT&T's core mission. Ultimately, our team was awarded the People's Choice Award for being unanimously voted the best overall product offering by our peers.

On top of my contribution to the project's content as the Creative Director, I served as the team's appointed leader. Therefore, I was tasked with a number of additional duties, such as managing the team's progress and quality of work; serving as our team's representative in all communications; meeting with our professor on behalf of the team to seek feedback and critique; all final editing and formatting; and submitting all final documents.

projects.title: Baylor University Instagram Takeover: Christmas on 5th Street 2019
projects.description:
As a Marketing Coordinator for the Baylor Activities Council (BAC), I worked directly with Baylor's Social Media Specialist and the BAC's Vice President for Marketing to instigate, plan, shoot, co-star in, and post a story takeover on Baylor University's official Instagram. This takeover showcased one of Baylor's largest annual events, Christmas on 5th Street, from an insider's perspective: that of a current undergraduate student working on the event. This included highlights of the 24 hours of setup leading up to the event, as well as a showcase of the event itself, including its various performances, rides, games, and other happenings.

On August 7, 2020, this takeover was referenced as #3 in “A Roundup of our Favorite Baylor Instagram Takeovers” by Baylor Proud, the official blog of Baylor University.

Length - 7 minutes and 33 seconds
Story Posts - 41

projects.title: Chili Cook-Off and Bed Races (CCOBR) 2019
projects.description:
Chili Cook-Off and Bed Races (also known as "CCOBR") is an annual, all-university, fall-time event taking place on Baylor University's campus, prominently featuring a chili cook-off and hospital bed races. The event is organized and executed through collaboration between Baylor University's Theta Kappa chapter of Chi Omega (Chi-O), Theta Nu chapter of Alpha Tau Omega (ATO), and the Baylor Activities Council (BAC). In 2019, CCOBR attracted an audience of 1,500+ attendees in one night, including 11 chili cook-off teams and 44 bed races teams.

As the BAC Marketing Coordinator for this event, I worked with BAC, Chi-O, and ATO Program Managers to develop an event identity as well as create and execute various marketing strategies (physical, digital, and guerrilla) campus-wide. These included a coordinated Instagram-based social media campaign across three distinct accounts; a bed races-themed guerrilla marketing effort; a one-and-a-half week-long t-shirt sales effort; the documentation of philanthropy-associated guests for future public relations uses; and handheld photography and videography during the event.

projects.title: FIJI Fright Night 2019
projects.description:

In 2019, FIJI Fright Night attracted an audience of 6,500+ attendees over the course of three days.

As the BAC Marketing Coordinator for this event, I worked with BAC and FIJI Program Managers to develop a positive and distinct event identity as well as create and execute various marketing strategies (physical, digital, and guerrilla) campus-wide. These included a coordinated Instagram-based social media campaign across three distinct accounts; having and documenting Baylor University's president as the inaugural guest through the haunted house; the planning, filming, and editing of four event hype videos; a three-day "IT Chapter Two" themed guerrilla marketing effort; a week-long t-shirt sales effort; and both handheld and drone photography/videography before and during the event.

projects.title: Operations Management Audit: Mission Waco
projects.description:
As a requirement for Baylor University's "Introduction to Operations Management" course (MGT 3325), my team of three undergraduate students and I were tasked with completing a semester-long project: an audit of all aspects pertaining to a local business's operations management. The project required that we meet with a representative of a chosen local business, gather information via interview and outside research, and deliver both a 10+ page report and an accompanying 12-15 minute long verbal presentation in-class.

After continued communication with Mission Waco (a local non-profit business) and diligent work, my team submitted our final deliverables more than a week early and our project was awarded first place in the class. We were personally commended for the quality of our analysis, devotion to the project, and commitment to communicating clearly with our professor.

On top of my contribution to the project's content, I served as the team's appointed leader. Therefore, I was tasked with a number of additional duties, such as managing the team's progress and quality of work; the creation of weekly status updates; meeting with our professor on behalf of the team to seek feedback and critique; all final editing and formatting; and submitting all final documents.

projects.title: ¡Parranda! 2019
projects.description:
¡Parranda! (now "¡Fiesta!") is an annual, all-university cultural celebration on Baylor University's campus, highlighting the diversity and vivacity of Latin America. The event immersed community members in the diverse cultures of Central and South America (including Mexico, Colombia, and Argentina) through its cuisine, interactive art, and live music and dance performances. ¡Parranda! was organized and executed through collaboration between Baylor University's Hispanic Student Association (HSA) and the Baylor Activities Council (BAC), reaching more than 750 people from the Baylor and Waco communities in 2019.

For ¡Parranda!, I served as a Program Manager for the BAC, working with other BAC and HSA members, on-campus authorities, and third-party vendors to create, advance, and execute the event from its formation to its completion.

publications.title: Employee Value Proposition and Benefits: Past, Present, and Future Connections
publications.publishedAt: Cornell Center for Advanced Human Resource Studies (CAHRS) · Jun 23, 2023
publications.description: Employee value propositions (EVPs) reflect the putative appeal of the financial and non-financial rewards employers offer to current and prospective employees. Research shows that carefully crafted EVPs play an important role in attracting and retaining top talent. This study focuses on one component of EVPs: employee benefits. Using data from 16 major CAHRS partner firms in 14 different industries, it explores the tactics used by large organizations to reinforce and refresh the perceived value of employee benefits.

publications.title: How Do Modern Business Practices Introduce Barriers to Hiring and Retaining “Hidden Workers”?
publications.publishedAt: Cornell Center for Advanced Human Resource Studies (CAHRS) · Dec 1, 2022
publications.description: Abstract: Within America’s increasingly competitive talent pool lies a large, underutilized, and greatly unsupported population: “hidden workers.” These are individuals who are willing and able to work but possess one or more barriers that contradict with employers’ profiles of a “viable” candidate, therefore struggling to find full-time employment. The term “hidden workers” encompasses a broad range of individual circumstances but can be generalized into a few categories: older workers; caregivers of children or elders; the formerly incarcerated or recovered substance users; those with physical or mental health issues; military veterans who lack civilian licenses or certifications; and immigrants or refugees who lack regional language skills. Though these workers may seem unfavorable from a more traditional recruiting perspective, organizations which actively hire hidden workers are less likely to face talent shortages and more likely to close skills gaps, proving that supporting them is both a strong moral objective and a strong business case. This executive summary seeks to identify key ways in which hidden workers are disproportionately challenged by modern business practices, highlighting how employers may actively work to mitigate the adverse effects of said practices while supporting hidden workers throughout the hiring, re-entering, and retention processes.

publications.title: What Can Organizations Do to Create an Environment That Supports and Retains Neurodiverse Employees?
publications.publishedAt: Cornell Center for Advanced Human Resource Studies (CAHRS) · Nov 1, 2022
publications.description: Abstract: Neurodiverse individuals are currently one of the most underemployed minority groups: in the United States, general unemployment for neurodiverse individuals is 30-40%, while up to 85% of people on the autism spectrum are unemployed. An increasing number of organizations are zooming in on this issue and aiming to intentionally support, engage, and retain neurodiverse individuals through the implementation of programs, cultures, and environments. However, a vast majority of these efforts are still in their infancy and their effectiveness is largely unknown. This whitepaper seeks to address how employers can most effectively include their neurodiverse employees in the modern workplace through the examination of current academic and business research; neurodiversity and disability theory; and case studies.

publications.title: Best Practices to Create a Feedback-Friendly Culture
publications.publishedAt: Cornell Center for Advanced Human Resource Studies (CAHRS) · Nov 1, 2022
publications.description: Abstract: During the early and mid-2010s, early adopters (such as Kelly Services, Adobe, Deloitte, and PwC) abandoned annual performance management methodologies in favor of continuous feedback systems. This was largely done to move away from feedback which punishes employees based on past performance and towards ongoing developmental feedback. Now, approximately 70% of multinational companies are using or moving towards a similar model. Not only does this signify a huge change in performance management, but it also exemplifies how regular feedback is becoming more and more common in the workplace. It is now critical that managers and employees understand how to give and receive feedback on a daily basis in order to remain effective and content. In this whitepaper, we aim to address this skill need by recommending methodologies and practices for giving and receiving feedback and highlighting key aspects of feedback-friendly organizational cultures.

publications.title: Business intelligence systems and operational capability: an empirical analysis of high-tech sectors
publications.publishedAt: Industrial Management and Data Systems · May 4, 2020
publications.description:
Purpose – In this research, we empirically examine the impact of Business Intelligence (BI) systems on operational capability in high-tech sectors. We also seek to understand the contextual factors that facilitate the
adoption of BI systems.
Design/methodology/approach – We adopt Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and event study methodology, and analyze the financial data for a sample of 144 US firms which adopted BI systems from 2005–2014, and compare them to control firms without BI systems.
Findings – We find that the implementation of BI systems leads to higher operational capability, particularly for large high-tech firms with high technology intensity. We further show that technology intensity and firm size are important contextual factors for firms to reap the benefits of BI systems.
Practical implications – We demonstrate how benefits from the adoption of BI systems are likely to be strengthened. The benefits of BI systems depend on firms’ technology intensity and firm size of high-tech firms.
Accessing relevant and timely reports for decision-making is particularly important in the highly dynamic, volatile and competitive high-tech sectors.
Originality/value – We contribute to the literature by providing empirical evidence that the adoption of BI systems can improve firms’ operational capability and show that technology intensity and firm size are important contextual factors for firms to reap the benefits of BI systems. We advance the understanding regarding the contextual factors in which firms are more likely to gain additional benefits from their adoptions of BI systems.

publications.title: Quality management and international trade: institutionalization of quality standards and performance outcomes in China
publications.publishedAt: Journal of Shipping and Trade · May 22, 2018
publications.description: Although the original purpose for quality management standards such as ISO 9000 was to facilitate international trade, their effectiveness is widely questioned recently. In the literature, it has been commonly argued that institutionalization of quality standards as time goes by is a major reason behind their ineffectiveness. We explored this issue by using recent data from stock-listed firms in China. Following previous studies in this area, we examined the impact of quality management standards on the cost-efficiency and sales performance of adopting firms from 2000 to 2014. We explored if such an impact is contingent on the level of institutionalization as evidenced by the time of certifications. We show that the time of quality certifications in China has a negative impact on the effectiveness of standards in improving cost-efficiency. However, we did not find a similar weakening impact on sales performance. Overall, we find evidence of the deteriorating effects of quality management certifications in more recent years.

publications.title: The Impact of Uncertainty Shocks on the UK Economy
publications.description: This paper quantifies the economic impact of uncertainty shocks in the UK using data that span the recent Great Recession. We find that uncertainty shocks have a significant impact on economic activity in the UK, depressing industrial production and GDP. The peak impact is felt fairly quickly at around 6-12 months after the shock, and becomes statistically negligible after 18 months. Interestingly, the impact of uncertainty shocks on industrial production in the UK is strikingly similar to that of the US both in terms of the shape and magnitude of the response. However, unemployment in the UK is less affected by uncertainty shocks. Finally, we find that uncertainty shocks can account for about a quarter of the decline in industrial production during the Great Recession.

projects.title: A study on Investment Analysis of selected IT Stocks Listed in NSE
projects.description:
Conducted a comprehensive research project as part of my MBA curriculum under Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU), Belagavi.

The study focused on the investment analysis of selected IT sector stocks listed on the NSE, specifically TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech, and Tech Mahindra. Using secondary data and financial models like Sharpe Index, Treynor Index, and Jensen’s Alpha, the project evaluated the risk-adjusted performance and volatility of stocks.

Key tools included statistical analysis (Beta, Standard Deviation) and risk-return evaluation models to identify optimal investment opportunities in the IT sector.

This project strengthened my skills in investment decision-making, financial modeling, data analysis, and understanding of market dynamics.
